exercises.title: Gaussian Algorithm and Solvability
exercises.description:
Given is the linear system of equations:
$\begin{align}
2x_1 + 3x_2 - x_3 &= 5 \\
x_1 - x_2 + 2x_3 &= 1 \\
3x_1 + 2x_2 + x_3 &= 6
\end{align}$

a) Solve the system using the Gaussian algorithm
b) Determine the rank of the coefficient matrix
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Set up augmented matrix
$\left(\begin{array}{ccc|c}
2 & 3 & -1 & 5 \\
1 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\
3 & 2 & 1 & 6
\end{array}\right)$

Step 2: First elimination (row 1 as pivot)
Swap rows 1 and 2 for better pivot:
$\left(\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\
2 & 3 & -1 & 5 \\
3 & 2 & 1 & 6
\end{array}\right)$

Step 5: Back substitution
From row 2: $5x_2 - 5x_3 = 3 \Rightarrow x_2 = x_3 + \frac{3}{5}$
From row 1: $x_1 - x_2 + 2x_3 = 1$
$x_1 = 1 + x_2 - 2x_3 = 1 + (x_3 + \frac{3}{5}) - 2x_3 = \frac{8}{5} - x_3$

Step 6: General solution
$x_3 = t$ (free parameter)
$x_2 = t + \frac{3}{5}$
$x_1 = \frac{8}{5} - t$

Rank of coefficient matrix: $\text{rank}(A) = 2$

exercises.title: Eigenvalues of a 2×2 Matrix
exercises.description:
Given is the matrix $A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$.

a) Determine all eigenvalues of A
b) Calculate the corresponding eigenvectors
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Set up characteristic polynomial
$\det(A - \lambda I) = \det\begin{pmatrix} 3-\lambda & 1 \\ 2 & 2-\lambda \end{pmatrix}$
$= (3-\lambda)(2-\lambda) - 1 \cdot 2 = \lambda^2 - 5\lambda + 4$

Step 2: Calculate eigenvalues
$\lambda^2 - 5\lambda + 4 = 0$
Using the quadratic formula:
$\lambda_{1,2} = \frac{5 \pm \sqrt{25-16}}{2} = \frac{5 \pm 3}{2}$
$\lambda_1 = 4$, $\lambda_2 = 1$

Step 3: Eigenvector for λ₁ = 4
$(A - 4I)v = 0$:
$\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$
From first row: $-v_1 + v_2 = 0 \Rightarrow v_2 = v_1$
Eigenvector: $v^{(1)} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 4: Eigenvector for λ₂ = 1
$(A - I)v = 0$:
$\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$
From first row: $2v_1 + v_2 = 0 \Rightarrow v_2 = -2v_1$
Eigenvector: $v^{(2)} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 5: Answer
Eigenvalues: $\lambda_1 = 4$, $\lambda_2 = 1$
Eigenvectors: $v^{(1)} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $v^{(2)} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$

exercises.title: Diagonalization of a 3×3 Matrix
exercises.description:
Given is the matrix $B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

a) Check if B is diagonalizable
b) If yes, provide a diagonal matrix D and a transformation matrix P such that $P^{-1}BP = D$
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Characteristic polynomial
$\det(B - \lambda I) = \det\begin{pmatrix} 1-\lambda & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{pmatrix}$
Expansion along row 2:
$= (2-\lambda) \cdot \det\begin{pmatrix} 1-\lambda & 1 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{pmatrix}$
$= (2-\lambda)[(1-\lambda)^2 - 1] = (2-\lambda)(\lambda^2 - 2\lambda) = -\lambda(2-\lambda)^2$

Step 2: Eigenvalues
$\lambda_1 = 0$ (simple), $\lambda_2 = 2$ (double)

Step 3: Eigenvector for λ₁ = 0
$(B - 0I)v = Bv = 0$:
$\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \\ v_3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$
From row 2: $2v_2 = 0 \Rightarrow v_2 = 0$
From row 1: $v_1 + v_3 = 0 \Rightarrow v_3 = -v_1$
Eigenvector: $v^{(1)} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 4: Eigenvectors for λ₂ = 2
$(B - 2I)v = 0$:
$\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \\ v_3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$
From row 1: $-v_1 + v_3 = 0 \Rightarrow v_3 = v_1$
$v_2$ is freely choosable.
Eigenvectors: $v^{(2)} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $v^{(3)} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 5: Check diagonalizability
Dimension of eigenspace for $\lambda = 2$: $\dim(E_2) = 2$ = algebraic multiplicity
Since we have 3 linearly independent eigenvectors, B is diagonalizable.

Step 6: Transformation matrix and diagonal matrix
$P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $D = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$
It holds: $P^{-1}BP = D$

exercises.title: Basis and Dimension
exercises.description:
Given are the vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$:
$v_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $v_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$, $v_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$, $v_4 = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}$

a) Check if the vectors $v_1, v_2, v_3$ are linearly independent
b) Determine a basis of the subspace spanned by $\{v_1, v_2, v_3, v_4\}$
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Check linear independence of v₁, v₂, v₃
We solve $\alpha_1 v_1 + \alpha_2 v_2 + \alpha_3 v_3 = 0$:
$\alpha_1 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + \alpha_2 \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} + \alpha_3 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 2: Set up system of equations
$\begin{align}
\alpha_1 + 2\alpha_2 + \alpha_3 &= 0 \\
2\alpha_1 + \alpha_2 - \alpha_3 &= 0 \\
\alpha_1 + 3\alpha_2 + 2\alpha_3 &= 0
\end{align}$
Matrix: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 4: Back substitution
From row 2: $\alpha_2 + \alpha_3 = 0 \Rightarrow \alpha_2 = -\alpha_3$
From row 1: $\alpha_1 + 2(-\alpha_3) + \alpha_3 = 0 \Rightarrow \alpha_1 = \alpha_3$
Only the trivial solution $\alpha_1 = \alpha_2 = \alpha_3 = 0$ exists.
$\Rightarrow v_1, v_2, v_3$ are linearly independent.

Step 5: Basis of the spanned subspace
We check if $v_4$ is linearly dependent on $v_1, v_2, v_3$:
$v_4 = \beta_1 v_1 + \beta_2 v_2 + \beta_3 v_3$
$\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 3 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} = \beta_1 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + \beta_2 \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} + \beta_3 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 6: Solve the system
$\begin{align}
\beta_1 + 2\beta_2 + \beta_3 &= 3 \\
2\beta_1 + \beta_2 - \beta_3 &= 3 \\
\beta_1 + 3\beta_2 + 2\beta_3 &= 4
\end{align}$
Solution: $\beta_1 = 1, \beta_2 = 1, \beta_3 = 0$
$\Rightarrow v_4 = v_1 + v_2$
Since $v_4$ is linearly dependent, $\{v_1, v_2, v_3\}$ forms a basis of the subspace.
Dimension: 3

exercises.title: Gram-Schmidt Orthogonalization
exercises.description:
Given are the vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$:
$u_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $u_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $u_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$

Apply the Gram-Schmidt process to construct an orthonormal basis.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Normalize first vector
$v_1 = u_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$
$||v_1|| = \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2 + 0^2} = \sqrt{2}$
$e_1 = \frac{v_1}{||v_1||} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 2: Orthogonalize second vector
$v_2 = u_2 - \langle u_2, e_1 \rangle e_1$
$\langle u_2, e_1 \rangle = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
$v_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{2} \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 3: Normalize second vector
$||v_2|| = \sqrt{(\frac{1}{2})^2 + (-\frac{1}{2})^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} + 1} = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}} = \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}$
$e_2 = \frac{v_2}{||v_2||} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{2} \\ -\frac{1}{2} \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \end{pmatrix}$

Step 4: Orthogonalize third vector
$v_3 = u_3 - \langle u_3, e_1 \rangle e_1 - \langle u_3, e_2 \rangle e_2$
$\langle u_3, e_1 \rangle = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
$\langle u_3, e_2 \rangle = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}$

Step 5: Calculate v₃
$v_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \end{pmatrix}$
$= \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{6} \\ -\frac{1}{6} \\ \frac{1}{3} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \end{pmatrix}$

Step 6: Normalize third vector
$||v_3|| = \sqrt{\frac{4}{9} + \frac{4}{9} + \frac{4}{9}} = \sqrt{\frac{4}{3}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$
$e_3 = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\begin{pmatrix} -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{pmatrix}$

Orthonormal basis: $\left\{\begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{pmatrix}\right\}$

exercises.title: Matrix of a Linear Mapping
exercises.description:
Given is the linear mapping $f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ with
$f\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$, $f\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$, $f\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$

a) Determine the representation matrix of $f$
b) Calculate $\ker(f)$ and $\text{im}(f)$
c) Verify the dimension formula
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a) - Determine representation matrix
The representation matrix $A$ has as columns the images of the standard basis vectors:
$A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$
Since $f(x) = Ax$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}^3$.

Step 2: Part b) - Determine kernel
$\ker(f) = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^3 : Ax = 0\}$
Solve the homogeneous system:
$\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 3: Gaussian elimination for kernel
$\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$
Swap rows: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$
$R_2 - 2R_1$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & -5 & -5 \end{pmatrix}$
Divide $R_2$ by $-5$: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 4: Back substitution for kernel
From row 2: $x_2 + x_3 = 0 \Rightarrow x_2 = -x_3$
From row 1: $x_1 + 3x_2 + 2x_3 = 0 \Rightarrow x_1 = -3x_2 - 2x_3 = 3x_3 - 2x_3 = x_3$
$\ker(f) = \text{span}\left\{\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\right\}$
$\dim(\ker(f)) = 1$

Step 5: Determine image
$\text{im}(f) = \text{span}\{A\text{-columns}\} = \text{span}\left\{\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}\right\}$
Check linear independence of first two columns:
$\det\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = 6 - 1 = 5 \neq 0$
The first two columns are linearly independent.
$\text{im}(f) = \mathbb{R}^2$, $\dim(\text{im}(f)) = 2$

Step 6: Part c) - Verify dimension formula
$\dim(\mathbb{R}^3) = \dim(\ker(f)) + \dim(\text{im}(f))$
$3 = 1 + 2 = 3$ ✓
The dimension formula is satisfied.

exercises.title: Determinant and Cramer's Rule
exercises.description:
Given is the matrix $C = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 5 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 & 8 \end{pmatrix}$ and the system $Cx = b$ with $b = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}$.

a) Calculate $\det(C)$ using expansion along the first row
b) Solve the system using Cramer's rule
c) Determine $\det(C^{-1})$
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a) - Calculate determinant
$\det(C) = 1 \cdot \det\begin{pmatrix} 5 & 3 \\ 0 & 8 \end{pmatrix} - 2 \cdot \det\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 8 \end{pmatrix} + 3 \cdot \det\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$
$= 1 \cdot (5 \cdot 8 - 3 \cdot 0) - 2 \cdot (2 \cdot 8 - 3 \cdot 1) + 3 \cdot (2 \cdot 0 - 5 \cdot 1)$
$= 1 \cdot 40 - 2 \cdot 13 + 3 \cdot (-5) = 40 - 26 - 15 = -1$

Step 2: Part b) - Apply Cramer's rule
Since $\det(C) = -1 \neq 0$, the system has a unique solution.
$x_1 = \frac{\det(C_1)}{\det(C)}$, $x_2 = \frac{\det(C_2)}{\det(C)}$, $x_3 = \frac{\det(C_3)}{\det(C)}$
where $C_i$ is the matrix with the $i$-th column replaced by $b$.

Step 3: Calculate $\det(C_1)$
$C_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 5 & 3 \\ 3 & 0 & 8 \end{pmatrix}$
$\det(C_1) = 1 \cdot \det\begin{pmatrix} 5 & 3 \\ 0 & 8 \end{pmatrix} - 2 \cdot \det\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 8 \end{pmatrix} + 3 \cdot \det\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ 3 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$
$= 1 \cdot 40 - 2 \cdot 7 + 3 \cdot (-15) = 40 - 14 - 45 = -19$
$x_1 = \frac{-19}{-1} = 19$

Step 5: Part c) - Determinant of inverse
$\det(C^{-1}) = \frac{1}{\det(C)} = \frac{1}{-1} = -1$
In general: $\det(A^{-1}) = \frac{1}{\det(A)}$ for invertible matrices.

Step 6: Final results
a) $\det(C) = -1$
b) Solution: $x = \begin{pmatrix} 19 \\ -6 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$
c) $\det(C^{-1}) = -1$

exercises.title: Definiteness of Quadratic Forms
exercises.description:
Given is the quadratic form $q(x) = x_1^2 + 4x_1x_2 + 4x_2^2 + 2x_2x_3 + x_3^2$ on $\mathbb{R}^3$.

a) Determine the associated symmetric matrix $A$
b) Check the definiteness of $q$ using the principal minor criterion
c) Determine an orthogonal basis that diagonalizes $q$
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a) - Determine symmetric matrix
$q(x) = x^T A x$ with $A = \begin{pmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12} & a_{13} \\ a_{12} & a_{22} & a_{23} \\ a_{13} & a_{23} & a_{33} \end{pmatrix}$
From $q(x) = x_1^2 + 4x_1x_2 + 4x_2^2 + 2x_2x_3 + x_3^2$:
$a_{11} = 1$, $a_{22} = 4$, $a_{33} = 1$
$2a_{12} = 4 \Rightarrow a_{12} = 2$
$2a_{23} = 2 \Rightarrow a_{23} = 1$
$2a_{13} = 0 \Rightarrow a_{13} = 0$
$A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 2: Part b) - Calculate principal minors
$M_1 = a_{11} = 1 > 0$
$M_2 = \det\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} = 4 - 4 = 0$
$M_3 = \det(A) = \det\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 3: Calculate $M_3$
$M_3 = 1 \cdot \det\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} - 2 \cdot \det\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} + 0$
$= 1 \cdot (4 - 1) - 2 \cdot (2 - 0) = 3 - 4 = -1 < 0$
Principal minors: $M_1 = 1 > 0$, $M_2 = 0$, $M_3 = -1 < 0$
Since $M_2 = 0$, the form is indefinite (neither positive nor negative definite).

Step 4: Part c) - Determine eigenvalues of A
Characteristic polynomial:
$\det(A - \lambda I) = \det\begin{pmatrix} 1-\lambda & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1-\lambda \end{pmatrix}$
$= (1-\lambda)[(4-\lambda)(1-\lambda) - 1] - 2[2(1-\lambda)]$
$= (1-\lambda)[4-5\lambda+\lambda^2-1] - 4(1-\lambda)$
$= (1-\lambda)(\lambda^2-5\lambda+3) - 4(1-\lambda)$
$= (1-\lambda)(\lambda^2-5\lambda-1)$

Step 5: Calculate eigenvalues
$\lambda_1 = 1$
$\lambda^2 - 5\lambda - 1 = 0$
$\lambda_{2,3} = \frac{5 \pm \sqrt{25+4}}{2} = \frac{5 \pm \sqrt{29}}{2}$
$\lambda_2 = \frac{5 + \sqrt{29}}{2} \approx 5.19 > 0$
$\lambda_3 = \frac{5 - \sqrt{29}}{2} \approx -0.19 < 0$
Since there are positive and negative eigenvalues, the form is indefinite.

Step 6: Determine eigenvectors (example for $\lambda_1 = 1$)
$(A - I)v = 0$:
$\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \\ v_3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$
From row 3: $v_2 = 0$
From row 1: $2v_2 = 0$ (satisfied)
From row 2: $2v_1 + v_3 = 0 \Rightarrow v_3 = -2v_1$
Eigenvector: $v^{(1)} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 7: Final results
a) $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$
b) The form is indefinite (principal minors: $1, 0, -1$)
c) Eigenvalues: $1, \frac{5 \pm \sqrt{29}}{2}$ with corresponding orthogonal eigenvectors

exercises.title: Various Matrix Norms
exercises.description:
Given is the matrix $M = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

a) Calculate the row sum norm $\|M\|_\infty$
b) Calculate the column sum norm $\|M\|_1$
c) Estimate the spectral norm $\|M\|_2$
solutionSteps:
Step 3: Part c) - Estimate spectral norm
The spectral norm is $\|M\|_2 = \sqrt{\rho(M^T M)}$, where $\rho$ is the spectral radius.
Alternatively: $\|M\|_2 \leq \sqrt{\|M\|_1 \cdot \|M\|_\infty} = \sqrt{5 \cdot 6} = \sqrt{30} \approx 5.48$

Step 4: More precise estimate
For a better estimate we calculate $M^T M$:
$M^T = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$
$M^T M = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 14 & 5 \\ 2 & 5 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 5: Estimate spectral radius
The largest eigenvalue of $M^T M$ lies between the smallest and largest Gershgorin circle:
Row 1: Center 5, radius $1+2=3$, interval $[2,8]$
Row 2: Center 14, radius $1+5=6$, interval $[8,20]$
Row 3: Center 5, radius $2+5=7$, interval $[-2,12]$
Largest eigenvalue $\leq 20$, so $\|M\|_2 \leq \sqrt{20} \approx 4.47$

Step 6: Final results
a) $\|M\|_\infty = 6$
b) $\|M\|_1 = 5$
c) $\|M\|_2 \leq \sqrt{30} \approx 5.48$ (rough bound) or $\|M\|_2 \leq \sqrt{20} \approx 4.47$ (Gershgorin)

exercises.title: SVD of a 2×3 Matrix
exercises.description:
Given is the matrix $N = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$.

a) Calculate $N^T N$ and determine its eigenvalues
b) Determine the singular values of $N$
c) Provide an orthogonal matrix $V$ such that $N^T N V = V \Sigma^2$
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a) - Calculate $N^T N$
$N^T = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$
$N^T N = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 6 & 4 \\ 6 & 4 & 4 \\ 4 & 4 & 8 \end{pmatrix}$

Step 2: Characteristic polynomial of $N^T N$
$\det(N^T N - \lambda I) = \det\begin{pmatrix} 10-\lambda & 6 & 4 \\ 6 & 4-\lambda & 4 \\ 4 & 4 & 8-\lambda \end{pmatrix}$
By expansion (extensive calculation):
$\chi(\lambda) = -\lambda^3 + 22\lambda^2 - 80\lambda = -\lambda(\lambda^2 - 22\lambda + 80)$

Step 3: Calculate eigenvalues
$\lambda_1 = 0$
$\lambda^2 - 22\lambda + 80 = 0$
$\lambda_{2,3} = \frac{22 \pm \sqrt{484 - 320}}{2} = \frac{22 \pm \sqrt{164}}{2} = \frac{22 \pm 2\sqrt{41}}{2} = 11 \pm \sqrt{41}$
$\lambda_2 = 11 + \sqrt{41} \approx 17.40$
$\lambda_3 = 11 - \sqrt{41} \approx 4.60$

Step 4: Part b) - Determine singular values
The singular values are $\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i}$ (for $\lambda_i > 0$):
$\sigma_1 = \sqrt{11 + \sqrt{41}} \approx 4.17$
$\sigma_2 = \sqrt{11 - \sqrt{41}} \approx 2.14$
$\sigma_3 = \sqrt{0} = 0$
Since $N$ is a $2 \times 3$ matrix, it has at most 2 non-zero singular values.

Step 5: Part c) - Eigenvectors of $N^T N$
For $\lambda_1 = 0$:
$(N^T N)v = 0$ leads to an eigenvector $v^{(1)}$ (calculation extensive)
For $\lambda_2, \lambda_3$: Corresponding eigenvectors $v^{(2)}, v^{(3)}$
The matrix $V$ has these orthonormal eigenvectors as columns.

Step 6: Simplified representation
Without explicit calculation of all eigenvectors:
$V$ is a $3 \times 3$ orthogonal matrix with $V^T (N^T N) V = \text{diag}(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3)$
$\Sigma^2 = \text{diag}(\sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2, \sigma_3^2) = \text{diag}(\lambda_2, \lambda_3, 0)$

Step 7: Final results
